chapters.why: God creates the world by his word and makes humanity, male and female, in his image. The foundation of the Bible's teaching on God, creation, and human dignity.
The first disobedience, its consequences, and the first hint of hope in the promise about the woman's seed. Everything that goes wrong in the Bible's story traces back here.
After the flood God makes a covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, and grounds the value of human life in the image of God.
God calls Abram and promises him a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth. The hinge on which the whole Bible turns from the world's story to Israel's.
Abram believes the LORD and it is credited to him as righteousness, and God binds himself by covenant in a strange night ceremony. Paul builds his teaching on faith on this chapter.
God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, then provides a ram in his place. One of the most searching and most discussed stories in Scripture.
Jacob wrestles through the night with a mysterious man, is renamed Israel, and walks away limping and blessed. The nation takes its name from this encounter.
Joseph forgives his brothers and names God's providence over their evil, and he dies trusting God to bring Israel back to the promised land.
God appears in the burning bush, hears the cry of his people, sends Moses, and reveals his name, I AM WHO I AM.
The first Passover: the lamb, the blood on the doorframes, the death of Egypt's firstborn, and the night Israel goes free.
God divides the sea for Israel and destroys Pharaoh's army, the Old Testament's defining act of salvation.
At Sinai God offers the covenant and calls Israel to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, then descends on the mountain in fire.
The Ten Commandments, grounded in the words that open them: the LORD who brought Israel out of the house of slavery.
The golden calf, Israel's first great breach of the covenant, and Moses' intercession for the people.
God proclaims his name and character to Moses and renews the broken covenant, a passage quoted throughout the Old Testament.
The tabernacle is set up and the glory of the LORD fills it, the goal toward which the whole book moves.
The burnt offering, the whole gift wholly given, opens the book and introduces the laying on of hands and the language of atonement.
Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD, a stark lesson that nearness to a holy God is a gift that cannot be handled carelessly.
The food laws, the first of the clean and unclean chapters, grounded in the command to be holy because the LORD is holy.
The Day of Atonement, the book's center, with the high priest behind the veil and the scapegoat carrying sin away.
The law of blood, including the verse that explains why blood makes atonement: the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Holiness in ordinary life, from harvest to courtroom, including the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
The Sabbath year and the Jubilee, when debts, slaves, and land are released, grounded in God's ownership of the land.
The covenant's blessings and curses, ending with the promise that God will remember his covenant even in exile.
The first census counts the fighting men of the generation that left Egypt, setting up the contrast with chapter 26 that frames the whole book.
The Nazirite vow and the priestly blessing, one of the oldest and best-loved blessings in the Bible.
The people refuse to enter the land, Moses intercedes by appealing to God's character, and the wilderness sentence is pronounced. The turning point of the book.
Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and Aaron standing between the living and the dead to stop the plague.
Miriam and Aaron die, and Moses, striking the rock in anger, is told he will not bring the people into the land.
The bronze serpent lifted on a pole, which Jesus used to explain his own death in John 3.
Balaam's last oracles, including the star from Jacob and the scepter from Israel, later read as a promise of the Messiah.
The second census: none of the first generation is left except Caleb and Joshua, and a new generation stands ready.
Moses retells the failure at Kadesh-barnea, setting the tone for the whole book: the new generation must not repeat its parents' unbelief.
Moses warns against making any image of God, since Israel saw no form at Horeb, and foresees exile and return for a people who seek him with all their heart.
The Shema: the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with all its heart, soul, and strength, and teach these words to its children.
The wilderness as God's school, where Israel learned that man does not live on bread alone, and the warning against forgetting God in prosperity.
The law of the one place God will choose for worship, which shaped Israel's religion and later reforms.
The promise of a prophet like Moses, which the New Testament applies to Jesus.
The promise of return after exile and of hearts circumcised by God, and the call to choose life.
Moses dies on Mount Nebo in sight of the land, and the Torah closes by saying no prophet like him has yet arisen.
God commissions Joshua after Moses' death with the charge to be strong and courageous and to meditate on the law day and night. It sets the terms for the whole book.
Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute in Jericho, hides the spies and confesses faith in the LORD. She becomes a lasting picture of an outsider brought in by faith.
Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground as the priests carry the ark, echoing the Red Sea crossing and marking Joshua as Moses' true successor.
The fall of Jericho, won by obedience and worship rather than siege, and the first application of the ban. Central to both the book's faith and its hardest questions.
Achan's hidden theft brings defeat on the whole nation. A sober study of sin, corporate responsibility, and confession.
The summary of fulfillment: the LORD gave Israel the land and rest, and not one of his good promises failed.
The covenant renewal at Shechem, where Joshua calls Israel to choose whom they will serve and declares that he and his house will serve the LORD.
The book's key: a generation forgets the LORD, and the narrator lays out the cycle of apostasy and deliverance that the rest of the book follows.
Deborah, Barak, and Jael defeat Sisera's chariots, one of the book's clearest victories, told again in the poetry of chapter 5.
God calls fearful Gideon, patiently answers his tests, and begins to tear down the altar of Baal in Gideon's own family.
Abimelech's murderous grab for kingship and Jotham's fable show what happens when a man makes himself king without God.
Jephthah, an outcast, delivers Israel from Ammon, and his rash vow ends in one of the most painful stories in Scripture.
Samson's fall to Delilah and his death in the temple of Dagon close the stories of the judges.
The book ends in civil war and desperate improvisation, with the verdict that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Ruth's pledge to Naomi (1:16-17) is one of the great statements of loyalty in literature, and Naomi's bitter return sets up the whole book.
The chance meeting in the field of Boaz shows providence at work in ordinary life and introduces the kinsman-redeemer.
The threshing-floor scene is the book's turning point, where Ruth asks Boaz to act as redeemer and he promises to do so.
The legal hearing at the gate, the birth of Obed, and the genealogy reveal that this family story leads to King David.
Hannah's song sets out the book's theology of reversal and names the LORD's anointed king for the first time, while Eli's house is condemned.
The LORD calls the boy Samuel, and the word of God returns to Israel through a prophet.
The ark is captured and the glory departs from Israel, a disaster that shows God cannot be used as a weapon.
Israel asks for a king like the nations, and God grants the request while calling it a rejection of his own rule.
Saul disobeys, and Samuel announces that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the kingdom has been torn from him.
David is anointed, because the LORD looks at the heart, and the Spirit leaves Saul.
David defeats Goliath, trusting in the LORD's name rather than in weapons.
David spares Saul in the cave, refusing to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed.
David's lament over Saul and Jonathan sets the tone for his reign: he grieves the king who hunted him rather than celebrating his fall.
All Israel anoints David king, and he captures Jerusalem, which becomes the City of David and the center of Israel's life and hope.
The ark comes to Jerusalem amid joy and danger, joining the throne of David to the presence of the LORD.
God's covenant with David promises an everlasting house, kingdom, and throne, the root of the Bible's hope for the Messiah.
David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah mark the turning point of his reign and of the book.
Nathan's parable confronts the king, David confesses, and God forgives him while announcing the consequences that will follow.
Absalom's death and David's grief over him show the full cost of the sword that would not depart from his house.
David's song of deliverance, nearly identical to Psalm 18, gathers the whole story into praise of God as rock and refuge.
Solomon asks for a discerning heart rather than riches or long life, and God gives him wisdom, shown at once in the judgment between two mothers.
The ark enters the temple, the glory fills it, and Solomon prays one of the Bible's great prayers, asking God to hear from heaven even when his people sin and are carried into exile.
Solomon's heart turns to other gods, and God announces that the kingdom will be torn from his son, leaving one tribe for David's sake.
Rehoboam's harsh answer divides the kingdom, and Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, the sin that shadows the northern kingdom to its end.
Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and fire from the LORD answers, a showdown over who is truly God.
The exhausted Elijah flees to Horeb, where God meets him not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in a quiet whisper, and sends him back to work.
Ahab and Jezebel murder Naboth to take his vineyard, and Elijah pronounces judgment, showing God's concern for justice to the powerless.
Micaiah alone tells Ahab the truth against four hundred prophets, and Ahab dies in battle just as the word of the LORD said.
Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives his cloak and a double portion of his spirit, marking the succession of prophetic ministry.
Naaman, an Aramean commander, is healed of skin disease by washing in the Jordan and confesses the God of Israel, a story Jesus later cites.
Jehu is anointed king and destroys Joram, Ahaziah, and Jezebel, fulfilling Elijah's word against the house of Ahab.
Athaliah tries to wipe out the royal line of Judah, and the rescue and crowning of the boy Joash keeps David's line alive.
Samaria falls to Assyria, and the narrator explains at length why the northern kingdom went into exile.
Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD, Isaiah answers, and Jerusalem is delivered.
The Book of the Law is found in the temple, and Josiah's response begins the greatest reform in Judah's history.
Jerusalem falls, the temple burns, and the people go into exile, yet the book ends with Jehoiachin released and fed at the king's table.
The genealogies begin with Adam, not Abraham, placing Israel's story inside the story of all humanity and all the nations.
The list of those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile connects the ancient genealogies to the Chronicler's own community and its temple service.
Saul's death is told with a theological verdict: he died for his unfaithfulness, and the LORD turned the kingdom to David.
The first attempt to move the ark ends in Uzzah's death, teaching that zeal for God must honor God's holiness and his ordered ways.
The ark arrives in Jerusalem, and David appoints Levites to lead continual praise, with a psalm of thanks that becomes the book's model of worship.
God promises David an everlasting dynasty and a son who will build God's house, the promise that shapes the rest of Chronicles.
David's sinful census leads to the choice of the temple site at Ornan's threshing floor, where judgment is stopped by sacrifice.
David leads Israel in generous giving and offers a great prayer of praise that confesses everything as God's, before Solomon takes the throne.
Solomon asks for wisdom at Gibeon, and the Chronicler sets the tone for his reign: a king whose greatness is God's gift.
Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to hear from heaven whenever his people pray toward this house, a prayer the rest of the book tests.
Fire and glory fill the temple, and God answers Solomon with the promise of 7:14 and a warning of exile.
Rehoboam's harsh answer divides the kingdom, a turning point the Chronicler traces to God's word through Ahijah.
Jehoshaphat's prayer in the face of invasion and the victory won by singing show the book's theology of trust in its clearest form.
Hezekiah's Passover invites all Israel, north and south, back to the house of God, and God heals a people who were not ritually ready.
Manasseh's captivity, prayer, and restoration show that no one is beyond the reach of repentance.
Jerusalem falls after long mercy, the land keeps its Sabbaths, and Cyrus's decree leaves the door open for return.
Cyrus's decree fulfills the word spoken through Jeremiah and begins the return from exile, told with echoes of the first exodus.
The altar is rebuilt and the foundation laid, and joy and weeping rise together as the old men remember Solomon's temple.
Darius confirms Cyrus's decree, the temple is finished and dedicated in 515 BC, and the returned exiles keep the Passover.
Ezra is introduced as a scribe devoted to studying, practicing, and teaching the law, and Artaxerxes commissions him.
Ezra's prayer of confession, in which the leader stands with his guilty people, is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament.
Nehemiah's prayer of confession, grounded in God's covenant promises to Moses, shows how the book's action begins in intercession.
Nehemiah risks his post before the king, receives leave to rebuild, and calls the people of Jerusalem to begin the work.
Nehemiah halts the project to confront the exploitation of poor Jews by their own nobles, showing that justice belongs to rebuilding.
Ezra reads the law to the whole people, the Levites explain it, and the people's weeping turns to joy in the Feast of Tabernacles.
A great prayer retells Israel's history as a story of God's faithfulness and the people's rebellion, and admits they are still slaves in their own land.
The book ends not in triumph but with renewed failure and renewed reform, and with Nehemiah asking God to remember him.
Esther becomes queen while hiding her identity, and Mordecai's unrewarded rescue of the king is recorded, setting up everything that follows.
Haman's decree to destroy the Jews reveals the depth of the threat and ties the story to the ancient conflict between Israel and Amalek.
Mordecai's challenge that Esther may have come to the kingdom “for such a time as this” and her decision to go to the king form the turning point of the book.
The king's sleepless night and Haman's humiliation are the book's clearest picture of hidden providence at work.
Esther names her people and her enemy, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
The day of destruction becomes a day of deliverance, and the feast of Purim is established.
The heavenly scene and the first test introduce the accuser's question and Job's great confession of worship in loss.
Job's lament sets the tone for the poem, bringing raw grief into the open before any argument begins.
Abandoned by friends and family, Job declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
A poem on the search for wisdom, which only God possesses, and which begins in the fear of the Lord.
Job's final oaths of innocence give a portrait of Old Testament righteousness in private and public life.
The LORD answers from the whirlwind, questioning Job about the foundations of the world.
Job's response, the rebuke of the friends, and the restoration of Job's household bring the book to its close.
The gateway to the book: the blessed life rooted in God's instruction, set against the way of the wicked.
The royal psalm of the king God calls his Son, quoted in the New Testament of Jesus' baptism, resurrection, and reign.
The lament Jesus quoted from the cross, which moves from forsakenness to praise among the nations.
The best-loved song of trust in the Bible, picturing the LORD as shepherd and host.
The great psalm of confession, linked by its heading to David's sin with Bathsheba.
A wisdom psalm that faces the prosperity of the wicked honestly and finds its answer in the sanctuary and the nearness of God.
The end of Book 3, where God's covenant with David seems to have failed, setting up the rest of the Psalter's answer.
The Old Testament text the New Testament quotes most often about Christ, the king seated at God's right hand and a priest forever.
The prologue states the book's purpose and its motto, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, and Wisdom first raises her voice in the streets.
The call to trust in the LORD with all your heart, and the teaching on the LORD's discipline that Hebrews 12 applies to Christian suffering.
Wisdom's great speech, including her presence with God before and during creation, a passage central to later Jewish and Christian reflection on the Word and on Christ.
The two banquets of Wisdom and Folly bring the opening section to its decisive choice.
The start of the Solomonic sayings shows the book's typical form: short, contrasting two-line proverbs.
Contains the much-quoted saying on training a child and the beginning of the words of the wise, with their links to Egyptian instruction.
Lemuel's mother's counsel on justice for the poor and the acrostic poem of the woman of noble character that closes the book.
The motto of futility and the poem of endless cycles set the book's question: what does a person gain from all his labor under the sun?
The royal experiment with pleasure, building, and wealth ends in despair over death, then turns to receive food and work as a gift from God's hand.
The famous poem of times and seasons, and the claim that God has set eternity in the human heart.
Counsel on careful worship and vows, and on the emptiness of loving money.
The shared fate of all, followed by the book's warmest call to enjoy life with the people and work God gives.
The poem on old age and death, and the epilogue's conclusion to fear God and keep his commandments.
The opening longing, the woman's own voice, and the first images of vineyard, flock, and king set the world of the whole book.
The spring invitation, the refrain of mutual belonging, and the first charge not to awaken love until the time is right.
The groom's praise of his bride and the image of the locked garden, the heart of the wedding sequence.
The night of hesitation and loss, and the woman's great poem of praise for her beloved.
The climax: love as strong as death, which many waters cannot quench and no wealth can buy.
The book's overture: God puts his people on trial, rejects worship without justice, and offers cleansing to those who repent.
Isaiah's vision of the Lord on his throne and his call, the source of the book's vision of God as the Holy One.
King Ahaz refuses to trust God, and Isaiah gives the sign of Immanuel, later read by Matthew as fulfilled in Jesus' birth.
The promise of light for Galilee and a child on David's throne whose names include Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace.
Hezekiah prays in the Assyrian crisis and Jerusalem is delivered, the great example of the trust the book calls for.
Comfort for the exiles: a voice in the wilderness, the frailty of flesh, and the everlasting word of God.
The Servant who is despised, pierced, and crushed for the sins of others, then vindicated, the Old Testament passage most closely tied to the cross.
God's promise of new heavens and a new earth, the vision the Bible's final chapters take up.
The call of Jeremiah, known before birth and sent to uproot and to plant, sets the terms for his whole ministry.
The temple sermon attacks trust in the temple as a charm and calls it a den of robbers, words Jesus later used.
The last and darkest of Jeremiah's confessions, where he feels deceived by God yet cannot stop speaking his word.
Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to build houses, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait for God's promised return.
The promise of a new covenant written on the heart, the Old Testament passage the New Testament most clearly claims as fulfilled in Christ.
King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, and the word of God is written again, a vivid picture of how the book itself came to be.
The fall of Jerusalem retold, closing with the release of the exiled king as a small sign that God's promise to David is not dead.
Introduces Jerusalem as a widow with no comforter and lets the ruined city speak her own confession and pain.
Faces the most difficult claim in the book, that the LORD himself acted as an enemy, and records the suffering of children without softening it.
The book's center, where a sufferer moves from despair to hope in God's unfailing loving devotion and faithfulness.
A communal prayer that ends with an open question, showing how the people of God pray when restoration has not yet come.
The inaugural vision of the glory of the LORD on a throne above the living creatures, shown to an exile far from the temple.
The glory rises from the temple and moves to its threshold and east gate, the beginning of God's departure from a defiled house.
The classic statement that each person answers for his own sin and that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls them to turn and live.
God judges Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David, the background to Jesus as the good shepherd.
The promise of cleansing, a new heart, and God's Spirit within his people, for the sake of his holy name.
The valley of dry bones: God's breath brings a dead nation to life, and two sticks become one kingdom.
The glory of the LORD returns from the east and fills the new temple, reversing the departure of chapters 10 and 11.
Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream sets out four kingdoms followed by a stone that becomes a mountain and fills the earth, the kingdom God himself establishes.
Three young men refuse to worship the golden statue and are delivered in the furnace, the book's classic picture of faith that will not bow.
Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration, told in his own voice, teach that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men and humbles the proud.
Daniel keeps praying despite the king's decree and is delivered from the lions, a story of quiet, costly faithfulness.
The vision of four beasts and the Ancient of Days, where one like the Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom, the source of Jesus' favorite title for himself.
Daniel's prayer of confession and the prophecy of seventy weeks, one of the most debated passages in the Bible.
The book closes with the clearest Old Testament promise of the resurrection of the dead.
The command to marry Gomer and the naming of the children set out the whole book's message of judgment and reversal.
The LORD's case against his unfaithful wife ends with the promise to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her, and betroth her forever.
Hosea buys back his wife, the book's clearest picture of costly, disciplined, restoring love.
A call to return, the complaint that Israel's loyalty is like morning mist, and the verse Jesus quoted: God desires mercy, not sacrifice.
God as the Father who taught Israel to walk, and whose compassion will not let him destroy his son.
The closing invitation to return and God's promise to heal and love freely.
The locust plague and the first sounding of the Day of the LORD show how Joel reads a natural disaster theologically, as a call to lament and seek God.
The book's turning point: the call to return with the whole heart, God's gracious answer, and the promise of the Spirit poured out on all people that Peter quoted at Pentecost.
The judgment of the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and the vision of Zion as refuge and source of life complete Joel's picture of the Day of the LORD.
The superscription sets Amos in time and place, and the oracles against the nations show a God who holds every people accountable for cruelty.
The trap closes: after condemning the neighbors, Amos turns on Israel and names its oppression of the poor in concrete detail.
The principle of election and accountability, and the chain of questions that explains why a prophet must speak.
The book's heart: a lament over Israel, the call to seek the LORD and live, the warning about the Day of the LORD, and the demand that justice roll like a river.
Amos's visions and his confrontation with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, show the prophet's calling and the cost of speaking.
The final vision of judgment gives way to the promise of David's restored tent, quoted by James at the Jerusalem council.
The whole book in one chapter: the charge against Edom, the Day of the LORD for all nations, and the promise that the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
Jonah's flight and the pagan sailors' turn to the LORD set up the book's central irony.
Jonah's prayer from the fish, the basis of Jesus' sign of Jonah, confesses that salvation is from the LORD.
Nineveh's repentance and God's relenting show that judgment announced is meant to lead to turning.
Jonah's anger at God's grace and God's closing question are the heart of the book.
Micah's attack on those who seize land and inheritances, and his first promise of a gathered remnant.
The indictment of rulers, priests, and prophets and the warning that Zion will be plowed like a field, remembered a century later in Jeremiah 26:18.
The nations stream to the mountain of the LORD and beat swords into plowshares, the same vision found in Isaiah 2:2-4.
The promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, cited in Matthew 2:6.
God's lawsuit against his people and the summary of what he requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.
The book's closing hymn to the God who pardons and keeps his promises to Abraham and Jacob.
The hymn to God's character sets the terms for the book: a jealous, avenging God who is also slow to anger, good, and a stronghold for those who trust him.
The poetic description of Nineveh's fall, with its river gates, plunder, and empty lion's den, is among the most vivid battle poetry in the Bible.
The woe against the city of blood and the comparison with Thebes explain why Nineveh falls, and the book's closing question leaves the reader weighing the cost of cruelty.
The two complaints and God's unsettling answer frame one of the Bible's most honest wrestlings with the problem of evil.
The command to wait for the vision, the declaration that the righteous will live by faith, and the five woes form the book's theological center.
The closing prayer, with its vision of God's coming and its resolve to rejoice in God though everything fails, is one of the great confessions of trust in Scripture.
The Bible's most concentrated description of the Day of the LORD, set against the idolatry and complacency of Jerusalem in Josiah's early reign.
The call to seek the LORD and humility, followed by judgment on the nations around Judah, shows both the reach of God's justice and the way of refuge.
The movement from woe on Jerusalem to the song of God rejoicing over his people is one of the great turns in the prophets.
The call to consider your ways and the people's rapid obedience show how God's word can reorder a community's priorities.
The promises of the latter glory, the shaking of the nations, and Zerubbabel as God's signet ring carry the book's hope beyond the building project to God's larger purposes.
The call to return and the first night vision, in which God declares that he is jealous for Jerusalem and will return to it with mercy.
Joshua the high priest, accused by Satan, is stripped of filthy garments and clothed in clean ones, a picture of forgiveness, and the promised Branch is announced.
The golden lampstand and the two olive trees, with the book's best-known word: not by might nor by power, but by God's Spirit.
Ten promises of a restored Jerusalem, where old people sit in the streets, children play, fasts become feasts, and the nations come seeking God.
The king who comes to Zion humble and riding on a donkey, the text the Gospels quote at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
The shepherd who is rejected and paid thirty pieces of silver, which Matthew connects with Judas's betrayal.
The spirit of grace poured out and the people's mourning for the one they have pierced, cited by John at the cross.
The day of the LORD, living waters flowing from Jerusalem, and the LORD as king over all the earth.
God's declaration of love and his rebuke of worthless worship set the terms of the whole book, and 1:11 promises that God's name will be great among the nations.
The chapter joins the corruption of the priesthood with unfaithfulness in marriage and gives one of the Old Testament's strongest statements of marriage as a covenant witnessed by God.
The promise of the messenger who prepares the way and the Lord who comes to his temple is quoted in the Gospels and applied to John the Baptist and Jesus.
The Old Testament's final words point back to the law of Moses and forward to Elijah, and the New Testament opens by answering them.
The genealogy and the virgin birth introduce Jesus as son of David, son of Abraham, and Immanuel, God with us.
The Beatitudes and Jesus' teaching on fulfilling the law open the Sermon on the Mount, among the most influential moral teaching in history.
The Lord's Prayer and Jesus' teaching on secret piety, treasure, and worry show the inner life of the kingdom.
The parables of the kingdom show how God's reign comes quietly, meets mixed responses, and grows toward a final harvest.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, Jesus speaks of building his church, and he begins to teach that he must suffer, die, and rise.
The Last Supper and Gethsemane show Jesus giving his body and blood for the forgiveness of sins and submitting to his Father's will.
The resurrection and the Great Commission complete the Gospel, with the risen Jesus claiming all authority and promising to be with his disciples always.
The title verse, John's preaching, Jesus' baptism, and the announcement of the kingdom set the terms for the whole book.
The parables of the kingdom and the stilling of the storm show how God's reign grows and raise the question of who Jesus is.
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi and the first passion prediction are the hinge of the Gospel.
Jesus teaches the way of the servant and gives the book's central statement of why he came, to give his life as a ransom for many.
The Olivet discourse foretells the temple's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man and calls disciples to watchfulness.
The crucifixion, where the centurion confesses Jesus as the Son of God, is the climax of Mark's portrait.
The empty tomb and the message of the resurrection close the book, and the question of its ending is best understood here.
The preface explains Luke's method, and the announcements to Zechariah and Mary, with Mary's song, set out the book's themes of reversal and fulfillment.
The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the shepherds, and Simeon's words about a light for the Gentiles anchor the good news in history and point to its reach.
Jesus' sermon at Nazareth from Isaiah 61 is his program statement for the whole ministry, and his rejection there foreshadows what follows.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show God's joy in finding the lost and expose the resentment of those who think they were never lost.
Zacchaeus's conversion and Jesus' statement that he came to seek and to save the lost lead into his entry into Jerusalem.
The empty tomb, the Emmaus road, and the ascension show the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures and sending his disciples to the nations.
The prologue presents Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh, and the first witnesses name him Lamb of God, Messiah, and Son of God.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that one must be born from above, and the chapter contains the Bible's most quoted summary of the gospel, John 3:16.
After feeding five thousand, Jesus declares himself the bread of life, and many disciples turn away while Peter confesses that Jesus has the words of eternal life.
Jesus raises Lazarus after declaring himself the resurrection and the life, the sign that sets the plot to kill him in motion.
At his last meal Jesus washes his disciples' feet and gives the new command to love one another as he has loved them.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples, and all who will believe through their word, that they may be one.
The empty tomb, the risen Jesus with Mary Magdalene and Thomas, and the Gospel's statement of its own purpose.
The risen Jesus gives the program of the book (1:8) and ascends, with the promise that he will return.
The Spirit comes at Pentecost, and Peter's sermon sets out the first public proclamation of the risen Christ.
Stephen's long speech retells Israel's history and his death marks the end of the Jerusalem period and introduces Saul.
Saul, the persecutor, meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.
Peter's visit to Cornelius opens the door to the Gentiles, with the Spirit falling on them as on the first believers.
The Jerusalem council decides that Gentile believers are saved by grace without circumcision, a turning point for the whole church.
Paul's speech in Athens shows how the gospel addresses a pagan audience with no knowledge of Israel's Scriptures.
Paul reaches Rome, and the book ends with the kingdom proclaimed boldly and without hindrance at the empire's heart.
The letter's theme (1:16-17) and its opening account of humanity's refusal to honor God.
The verdict that all have sinned, and the central statement of righteousness through faith and Christ's atoning death (3:21-26).
Abraham as the pattern of justification by faith and the father of Jewish and Gentile believers alike.
Peace with God, and the comparison of Adam and Christ that frames the human story.
Union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and freedom from the reign of sin.
Life in the Spirit, adoption, the hope of creation, and the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God's love.
The start of Paul's wrestling with Israel's unbelief and God's freedom in mercy.
The turn to the life of a people shaped by mercy, beginning with bodies offered as living sacrifices.
Sets out the letter's center: the message of the cross as God's power and wisdom, confronting a church divided by loyalty to leaders.
Leaders are servants and fellow workers, Christ is the only foundation, and the church is God's holy temple where his Spirit dwells.
Paul's longest discussion of marriage, singleness, and divorce, shaped by the conviction that the present form of the world is passing away.
On food sacrificed to idols, Paul sets knowledge against love and confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
Contains the earliest written account of Jesus instituting the Lord's Supper, set in a rebuke of a divided church meal.
The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good, and every member, especially the weaker, is needed.
The chapter on love, which judges every gift and every claim to knowledge by whether it is patient, kind, and humble.
The fullest New Testament teaching on the resurrection of Christ and of believers, and the earliest written list of resurrection appearances.
The God of all comfort, Paul's near-death ordeal in Asia, and the declaration that every promise of God is Yes in Christ.
The ministry of the new covenant, written by the Spirit, and the unveiled faces that are being transformed into the Lord's image.
Treasure in jars of clay: the light of God's glory in the face of Christ carried by fragile, afflicted messengers.
The hope of the resurrection body, the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation grounded in the great exchange of 5:21.
The grace of giving, modeled on Christ who though rich became poor, and the collection for the believers in Jerusalem.
Paul's vision of the third heaven, the thorn in his flesh, and the Lord's answer that his power is perfected in weakness.
Paul's astonishment at a different gospel and the story of his call, which establishes that his message came by revelation from Christ.
The Jerusalem meeting, the confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and the letter's central statement of justification by faith in Christ.
The argument from Abraham, the curse of the law borne by Christ, the law as a guardian, and the unity of all believers in Christ.
God sends his Son and his Spirit so that believers become sons and heirs; Paul's pastoral plea and the allegory of Hagar and Sarah.
Freedom in Christ, the warning against circumcision, and the works of the flesh set against the fruit of the Spirit.
One of the great passages of praise in the Bible, setting out God's plan to bring all things together in Christ and the blessings believers receive in him.
The classic statement of salvation by grace through faith, followed by the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile into one new humanity through the cross.
The turn from teaching to life: the unity of the Spirit, the gifts of the ascended Christ to build up the body, and the call to put on the new self.
Contains the most debated passage on Christian marriage, which ties husband and wife to the relationship between Christ and the church.
Closes the household instructions with children, parents, slaves, and masters, and gives the well-known picture of the armor of God.
Paul's thanksgiving and prayer, his report that chains have advanced the gospel, and his reflection that to live is Christ and to die is gain.
The Christ hymn (2:6-11), one of the central passages of the New Testament on who Christ is, set within a call to humility and unity.
Paul counts his own righteousness as loss in order to gain Christ and the righteousness that comes from God through faith.
Calls to rejoice, to pray instead of worrying, and to learn contentment, with Paul's thanks for the church's gift.
The hymn to Christ as the image of God, creator, head of the church, and reconciler of all things (1:15-20), with Paul's prayer and his account of his ministry.
Paul's answer to the false teaching: all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, the powers were disarmed at the cross, and the rules are shadows of the reality.
The new life of those raised with Christ, marked by putting off the old self and putting on love, peace, and thankfulness, with instructions for the household.
A compact picture of conversion in the first generation: the gospel coming in power and the Spirit, and Gentiles turning from idols to serve God and await his Son.
Paul's account of how he and his companions conducted themselves, one of the fullest pictures of his ministry and motives in any of his letters.
Instruction on holiness and daily work, and the passage on believers who have died and the Lord's coming (4:13-18).
The Day of the Lord coming like a thief, and a series of brief commands for church life, including rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks.
The promise of relief for the persecuted and judgment on their oppressors at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven.
The central and much-debated passage on the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, and the restrainer, followed by thanksgiving for God's choice of the church.
Paul's request for prayer and his instructions about members who refuse to work, with the reminder of his own example.
Paul's testimony of mercy to the worst of sinners gives the letter its gospel foundation and sets the tone for how Timothy must oppose false teaching.
Contains the confession of one God and one mediator, and the debated instructions on women in worship.
Sets out the character required of overseers and deacons and names the church the pillar and foundation of the truth, closing with an early Christian hymn.
Defends the goodness of creation against false asceticism and gives Timothy a portrait of faithful ministry.
The New Testament's fullest warning about the love of money, and a charge to fight the good fight of the faith.
Sets the letter's tone of courage and grace, with a rich summary of salvation by God's purpose and grace given in Christ before time began.
Calls Timothy to hand on the teaching, remember the risen Christ, and correct opponents with gentleness, and contains an early Christian saying about dying and reigning with Christ.
Contains the New Testament's central statement on the inspiration and usefulness of Scripture.
Paul's final charge to preach the word and his farewell: he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.
Sets out the qualifications of elders on Crete and describes the false teachers they must resist.
Grounds instructions for every group in the church in the grace of God that trains believers, and names Jesus Christ our great God and Savior.
Contains one of the New Testament's fullest summaries of salvation by mercy through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
The whole letter is one chapter: Paul's appeal for Onesimus, a slave who has become a brother, and his offer to take on Onesimus's debt himself.
The majestic opening: God's final word in the Son, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at God's right hand.
The Son shares our flesh and blood, tastes death for everyone, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest.
The Sabbath rest that remains, the living word of God, and the invitation to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
The sharpest warning against falling away, followed by the anchor of hope secured by God's oath.
Melchizedek and the eternal priesthood of Jesus, who always lives to intercede.
The tabernacle and the Day of Atonement read as pointers to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.
The great roll call of faith, from Abel to the unnamed martyrs.
Running the race with eyes fixed on Jesus, the discipline of the Father, and the unshakable kingdom.
It sets out the letter's themes, from trials and wisdom to the call to be doers of the word and the definition of pure religion.
The famous discussion of faith and deeds, and the sharpest New Testament rebuke of favoritism toward the rich.
The Bible's fullest reflection on the power of speech, and the contrast between earthly wisdom and the wisdom from above.
Judgment on oppressive wealth, patience until the Lord's coming, and the practice of prayer and anointing for the sick.
Praise for new birth into a living hope, the call to holiness, and redemption by the precious blood of Christ.
The church as living stones and a royal priesthood, and Christ as the suffering servant whose example his people follow.
The call to be ready with a defense of hope, and the difficult passage on Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison.
Joy in sharing Christ's sufferings, the only New Testament letter use of the name Christian, and the call to entrust oneself to a faithful Creator.
God's provision for life and godliness, the ladder of virtues, the transfiguration testimony, and the classic statement on how prophecy came from God.
The longest New Testament warning against false teachers, closely parallel to Jude.
The answer to scoffers about Christ's delayed return, the promise of a new heaven and earth, and the reference to Paul's letters as Scripture.
The prologue's eyewitness claim, and the teaching that God is light and that those who confess their sins are forgiven and cleansed.
Christ as advocate and atoning sacrifice, the old and new commandment, and the departure of the antichrists.
The Father's love in calling us his children, and love defined by Jesus laying down his life.
Testing the spirits, and the great statement that God is love, shown in the sending of his Son.
Faith that overcomes the world, God's testimony about his Son, and the letter's purpose of assurance.
The whole letter: truth and love held together, and the warning against teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
The whole letter: hospitality as partnership in the truth, and a warning against leadership that loves to be first.
The whole letter: the call to contend for the faith, the examples of judgment, the use of Enoch and the Moses tradition, and the great closing doxology.
John's commission on Patmos and the vision of the risen Christ among the lampstands, the First and the Last who holds the keys of death.
The first four messages to the churches, showing Christ's intimate knowledge of real congregations and his call to overcome.
The Lion who is a slain Lamb takes the scroll, and all creation worships him: the theological heart of the book.
The dragon's war against the woman and her child shows the spiritual conflict behind history.
The beasts from the sea and the land, the demand for worship, and the number 666.
The binding of Satan, the thousand-year reign, and the final judgment, the source of the millennial debates.
The new heaven and new earth and the holy city, where God dwells with his people and makes all things new.
The river and tree of life, and the closing promise and prayer for Christ's coming.
